A premise is a starting point — a statement, assumption, or idea that is accepted as true before anything else is built on top of it.

Think of it like the foundation of a house. You don't question the foundation while you're building the walls. You accept it as solid, and everything above it depends on it. A premise works the same way: it is the ground-level truth (or assumed truth) that supports whatever comes after it.

The word "premise" has three distinct but related meanings. You'll encounter all three in real life.

Meaning 1: In Logic and Arguments

In logic and reasoning, a premise is a statement that is presented as true in order to reach a conclusion.

Every argument has a structure:

  • You start with one or more premises.
  • You reason from them.
  • You arrive at a conclusion.

Example:

Premise 1: All human beings need food to survive.
Premise 2: Maria is a human being.
Conclusion: Therefore, Maria needs food to survive.

The two premises are the given facts. The conclusion is what follows logically from them. Notice that the conclusion is only as strong as the premises. If a premise is wrong, the whole argument falls apart.

This is why in debates and discussions, people often say things like:

  • "I reject your premise." → "I don't accept your starting assumption as true."
  • "Your argument is built on a false premise." → "Your conclusion is wrong because your starting point was wrong."

Meaning 2: In Everyday Language (Stories, Plans, Beliefs)

In everyday use, "premise" means the core assumption or central idea that something is based on. This could be a story, a business plan, a theory, a decision, or a belief system.

Examples:

  • "The premise of the movie is that a scientist builds a time machine and accidentally changes history."
    Here, "premise" means the basic setup — the fundamental idea the story is built on. If you reject that idea, the whole story doesn't work for you.
  • "The government's economic plan rests on the premise that lower taxes lead to more business growth."
    Here, "premise" means the foundational assumption the plan depends on. Whether the plan succeeds or fails partly depends on whether this premise is true.
  • "She made her decision on the premise that he was telling the truth."
    Here, "premise" means the assumed fact that guided her thinking.

In this usage, "premise" is almost synonymous with "assumption" or "basis," but it carries a slightly more formal and logical flavour — it implies that the idea in question is the logical starting point from which other things follow.

Meaning 3: A Building or Property (Almost Always Plural: "Premises")

This meaning is quite different from the first two, and it belongs mostly to legal and formal contexts.

"Premises" (note: almost always used in the plural) refers to a piece of land together with any buildings on it — essentially, a property or establishment.

Examples:

  • "Please leave the premises immediately." → Leave this building/property.
  • "Smoking is not permitted on the premises." → Not allowed in or around this building.
  • "The restaurant's premises were inspected by the health department." → The actual physical place the restaurant occupies.

You'll see this in legal documents, signs in shops and offices, and news reports. It sounds formal because it is — in casual speech, people usually just say "the building," "the place," or "the property."

One small but important note: You almost never say "on the premise" when talking about property. You say "on the premises." The plural form is the standard here.

The logical meaning (Meaning 1) and the everyday meaning (Meaning 2) are really the same idea at different scales of formality.

In both cases, a premise is something you accept as true first, so you can build something else on it. In formal logic, that "something else" is a conclusion. In everyday life, it could be a story, a plan, a policy, or a decision.

Think of it this way: every time someone says "assuming that... / based on the idea that... / given that..." — they are essentially introducing a premise.

These two words are opposites in logical thinking, and understanding them together makes both clearer:

  • A premise is what you start with — the input.
  • A conclusion is what you arrive at — the output.

The premise comes before. The conclusion comes after. The conclusion is justified by the premises. The premises are not justified by the conclusion — they stand on their own.

• "on the premise that" — based on the assumption that.
    "He invested all his money on the premise that the stock would rise."
  • "false premise" — a starting assumption that is not actually true.
    "The entire argument was built on a false premise."
  • "question the premise" — to challenge the starting assumption itself, rather than argue about what follows from it.
    "Before we debate this further, I want to question the premise of your question."
  • "the premise of [a story/show/film]" — the central idea or scenario the story is built around.
    "The premise of the show is that robots have developed feelings."
  • "on the premises" / "off the premises" — inside or outside the building/property.
    "No visitors are allowed on the premises after 6 PM."

—What it means
In logicA statement accepted as true, used as the starting point of an argument to reach a conclusion
In everyday useThe core assumption, central idea, or foundational belief that something else is built upon
As "premises" (property)A building and the land it sits on

The golden thread running through all uses: a premise is always a starting point — something laid down first, before anything else can stand.
